title: Capability Negotiation and Slice Orchestration Guidelines
author: Aisha Patel
body:
h1. Capability Negotiation and Slice Orchestration Guidelines

Summary

This page defines a cross-cutting pattern and a concrete API contract for capability negotiation between clients and Redwood inference services, together with a standards-compliant configuration model for adaptive GPU slice orchestration. The goal is to enable clients and the runtime to discover and negotiate acceptable tradeoffs (latency, fidelity, cost) at call time, and for the orchestration layer to map negotiated profiles to concrete scheduling and slice allocation decisions.

Why this exists

- Enable richer, backward-compatible client-server coordination for adaptive serving without per-customer custom code.
- Reduce failed requests and noisy retries by making capability expectations explicit.
- Provide a single canonical config surface that ties API-level negotiation to infra-level slice orchestration and telemetry.

Scope

This document covers:

- API-level request/response headers and JSON payloads for capability negotiation.
- Server-side behavior when negotiation succeeds/partially-succeeds/fails.
- An orchestration config model used by the GPU scheduler to allocate slices, prewarm kernels, and apply quantization profiles.
- Observability signals (SLIs, metrics, traces) required to validate correctness and SLO compliance.
- Rollout guidance, migration steps, and a short ADR summarizing key decisions.

This does not cover: client SDK ergonomics (see sdk-guides), private-deployment-specific network topology (see eng-private-deployments), or model architecture-specific kernel tuning (see runtime-architecture).

Design principles

- Explicitness: Capability expectations are explicit and machine-readable. No implicit assumptions.
- Graceful degradation: When perfect negotiation isn't possible the runtime should offer the closest compatible profile and flag it in the response.
- Observability-first: Every negotiation decision must emit telemetry to enable SLI-driven rollbacks.
- Incremental compatibility: New negotiation fields must be opt-in and follow semantic versioning semantics.

Core primitives

1) capability_profile (client-provided hint): A short, opaque token representing high-level preferences. Examples: "ultra-low-latency", "balanced-cost", "max-quality".
2) capability_constraints (optional object): Structured constraints the client requires (max_latency_ms, min_embedding_dim, allowed_fidelity_tiers).
3) offered_profile (server response): The profile the server offers after considering capacity and policies.
4) negotiation_status (server response): one of: accepted, degraded, rejected.

API: request and response contract

- Header: X-Redwood-Capability: <capability_profile>
- JSON payload (optional top-level field): negotiation { capability_constraints: { max_latency_ms, min_quality_score, cost_priority } }

Example request (curl):

curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Redwood-Capability: balanced-cost" \
  -d '{
    "input": "Summarize the product roadmap",
    "negotiation": {
      "capability_constraints": {
        "max_latency_ms": 1200,
        "min_quality_score": 0.85,
        "cost_priority": "medium"
      }
    }
  }'

Example server response (successful negotiation):

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "negotiation": {
    "offered_profile": "balanced-cost-v2",
    "negotiation_status": "accepted",
    "applied_slice": "slice-a3-p2",
    "estimated_cost_units": 0.42
  },
  "response": { "text": "Product roadmap summary..." }
}

Example server response (degraded):

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{
  "negotiation": {
    "offered_profile": "balanced-cost-v2-degraded",
    "negotiation_status": "degraded",
    "degradation_reasons": ["kernel_quantized","reduced_kv_cache"],
    "estimated_cost_units": 0.18
  },
  "response": { "text": "Condensed summary..." }
}

When negotiation is rejected:

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict
{
  "error": "capability-unavailable",
  "details": "Requested minimum latency cannot be satisfied under current capacity"
}

Server behavior and orchestrator contract

- Decision timeline:
  1) Validate capability_constraints schema; enforce quotas and rate limits.
  2) Compute candidate profiles based on model capability manifest, active quantization profiles, tenant policies, and current GPU capacity.
  3) Score candidates by (SLO gap, cost delta, fidelity delta) and select highest-scoring candidate.
  4) Reserve slice or queue request with priority based on negotiated profile.

- If a slice reservation is required, the orchestration API must be called with a standard payload (SliceAllocation) within 50ms of decision.
- If slicing cannot be fulfilled immediately, the runtime can return a degraded profile or a 202 Accepted with a status endpoint where the client may poll for completion.

SliceAllocation payload (YAML example used by orchestrator):

slice_id: slice-a3-p2
tenant_id: tenant-123
cpu_cores: 2
gpu_slices: 0.25
model_variant: redwood-llm-1.3-q4
kv_cache_mode: partial
prewarm_kernels: [fast-attention-v2]
expected_duration_ms: 800
priority: medium

Configuration table: negotiable fields

| parameter | type | default | allowed values | enforced by |
| max_latency_ms | int | 2000 | >=50 | API layer (validation) |
| min_quality_score | float | 0.7 | (0.0 - 1.0) | Model/ops policy |
| cost_priority | enum | "medium" | low/medium/high | Billing + routing |
| allowed_fidelity_tiers | list | ["standard"] | ["standard","high","lossy"] | Model manifest |
| fallback_policy | enum | "auto-degrade" | auto-degrade/reject/queue | Runtime/orch |

Integration points (who owns what)

- API gateway: schema validation, header extraction, rate limiting, basic scoring. Owner: eng-platform.
- Negotiation engine (service-level library): transforms constraints -> profiles. Owner: eng-serving-runtime.
- Orchestrator: slice allocation, reservation, prewarm. Owner: eng-infra (gpu-fleet-and-capacity).
- Billing adaptor: converts estimated_cost_units -> billing tokens. Owner: finance-and-legal.

Client behavior patterns

- Best-effort negotiation: clients should provide capability_profile header for preferred mode and a short constraint set. They must be prepared to accept degraded profiles and use response.negotiation.negotiation_status to adapt.
- Fallbacks: clients that cannot accept degraded responses must set fallback_policy: "reject" and prepare to handle 409 responses.
- Polling: when 202 Accepted is returned, clients may poll the provided status endpoint; exponential backoff recommended (start 100ms, max 3s, 5 attempts).

Observability requirements

Essential telemetry emitted per request:

- negotiation.request_profile (tag) - string
- negotiation.result_profile (tag) - string
- negotiation.status (metric) - {accepted,degraded,rejected}
- slice.allocation_latency_ms (histogram)
- slice.prewarm_time_ms (histogram)
- estimated_cost_units (gauge)
- negotiation.reasons (event/log array)

SLIs and thresholds (initial targets)

- Negotiation acceptance rate >= 97% (daily, per-tenant)
- P95 slice allocation latency < 75ms
- P99 end-to-end negotiation + model-inference latency within negotiated max_latency_ms 99% of the time for accepted profiles
- Degraded-negotiation-rate <= 2% for tier "gold" customers

Alerting rules (examples)

- Alert: negotiation-acceptance-drop
  - Trigger: 10m rolling window acceptance rate < 90% for global
  - Owner: eng-sre
- Alert: slow-slice-allocation
  - Trigger: P95 slice.allocation_latency_ms > 250ms
  - Owner: eng-infra

Performance and safety guardrails

- Negotiation must be CPU-light; the negotiation library must be implementable as a local fast path (no network call unless orchestrator reservation is required).
- A hard timeout of 150ms is enforced for the API negotiation loop. If negotiation exceeds the timeout the request should either proceed with last-known-good profile or return a degraded or 202 response based on fallback_policy.
- To prevent oscillation, once a client receives a degraded profile the runtime must not flip back to a higher-fidelity profile for the same session for at least 30s unless explicitly forced by client.

Rollout and migration plan

1) V1: server implements header-based capability_profile only (no constraints). Rollout to 10% of traffic. Collect telemetry.
2) V2: add structured capability_constraints; orchestrator accepts SliceAllocation and supports prewarm_kernels. Canary 5 tenants.
3) V3: add rejected/degraded handling and status endpoints. Expand to all non-enterprise tiers.
4) Enterprise opt-in: private deployments can opt-out or override orchestration hooks via local policy.

Migration checklist

- Update SDKs to surface X-Redwood-Capability header (deprecate older heuristics).
- Add synthetic tests that inject varying capacity conditions and validate negotiation_status distribution.
- Run game-day: induce GPU pressure and validate degraded negotiation emits reasons and that clients apply fallback_policy.

Security and privacy considerations

- Capability tokens are non-sensitive and may be logged; capability_constraints should avoid embedding PII. If client-specific policy is included, mark negotiation payload non-public and redact in logs.
- Orchestrator must validate tenant_id and not allow cross-tenant slice borrow without explicit admin policy.

Short ADR: decision summary

- Decision: Represent capability preferences as an optional header + optional structured constraints in the payload. Implement negotiation locally in the API layer and call the orchestrator only for concrete reservations.
- Rationale: minimizes latency for common-case decisions while preserving a canonical signal for the orchestrator when slices must be reserved.
- Alternatives considered: fully server-driven runtime (would reduce signal to clients) and client-side heavy negotiation (SDK divergence). Both rejected due to operational complexity.

Open questions

- Should we standardize a numeric fidelity score across models? (Follow-up: product/research working group to decide Q4 2026)
- How to express multi-model compositional constraints (tool-chains) succinctly? Proposal: compose capability_profiles using a small DSL; experiment in V3.

Appendix: example negotiation schema (JSON Schema excerpt)

{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "capability_profile": { "type": "string" },
    "capability_constraints": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "max_latency_ms": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 50 },
        "min_quality_score": { "type": "number", "minimum": 0, "maximum": 1 },
        "cost_priority": { "type": "string", "enum": ["low","medium","high"] }
      }
    },
    "fallback_policy": { "type": "string", "enum": ["auto-degrade","reject","queue"] }
  }
}

Related pages and references

- Service introspection and client-adaptive contracts (internal link) - reference for versioning rules.
- GPU slice scheduling playbook - reference for allocator knobs.
